section_summaries.epidemiology: Rabies is a zoonosis enzootic worldwide, except Antarctica and some islands, with an estimated annual mortality of 59,000, primarily in Asia and Africa. The domestic dog is the major reservoir and vector, causing >99% of human infections. Sylvatic rabies reservoirs include skunks, raccoons, foxes, and insectivorous bats in North America; foxes in the Arctic; mongooses in Caribbean islands; and vampire bats in Latin America. Bat lyssaviruses in the Americas are classic rabies genotype/species 1, while Old World bats harbor rabies-related lyssaviruses. Human rabies is often under-reported, with 43% of US cases in the last 10 years infected abroad, and 75% of indigenous infections due to bat rabies viruses. Rabid dogs typically have an incubation period of 2 weeks to 4 months, showing behavioral changes, fever, irritation at the bite site, and often paralytic or "dumb" rabies symptoms, with virus excretion in saliva for 2 or 3 days before signs appear.
section_summaries.pathogenesis: Rabies virus may replicate locally in myocytes before binding to acetylcholine receptors at neuromuscular junctions. It then enters peripheral motor neurons, transported retrogradely to the cell soma where it replicates and spreads trans-synaptically to the central nervous system (CNS). The virus remains intraneuronal, with massive replication in the brain. Centrifugal spread from the CNS along nerves infects salivary glands, lacrimal glands, skin, respiratory tract, and myocardium. In unvaccinated patients with rabies encephalomyelitis, no antibody response is typically detected in serum or CSF until the second week of illness. Histopathologic changes are usually mild, with furious rabies affecting the midbrain and medulla, and paralytic rabies affecting the spinal cord. Changes include ganglion cell degeneration, perineural and perivascular mononuclear cell infiltration, neuronophagia, glial nodules, and characteristic Negri bodies. After vaccination, viral glycoprotein induces neutralizing antibody, which is protective.
section_summaries.clinical_manifestations: After a variable incubation period (20-60 days, extreme range 4 days to >19 years), often shorter with facial or severe multiple bites, symptoms begin. The most suggestive prodromal symptom of rabies encephalitis is paresthesia and itching at the healed bite site. Early non-specific symptoms include fever, mood changes, and upper respiratory or gastrointestinal issues. Furious rabies, the more common presentation, involves pathognomonic hydrophobia or aerophobia, characterized by forceful, jerky inspiratory spasms provoked by water attempts or air drafts, coupled with terror. Other signs include episodic generalized arousal, hallucinations, aggression, meningism, cranial nerve lesions, upper motor neuron lesions, fasciculation, involuntary movements, hyperesthesia/hyperacusis, and autonomic dysfunctions like sweating, hypersalivation, lacrimation, and fluctuating blood pressure. Without intensive care, patients typically die within days of hydrophobia. Paralytic rabies is less distinctive, often misdiagnosed, and common with vampire and other bat-transmitted cases in the Americas. It involves flaccid paralysis (often in the bitten limb) ascending symmetrically or asymmetrically, with pain and fasciculation, leading to fatal paralysis of deglutitive and respiratory muscles; hydrophobia is rare. Prolonged survival with intensive care can lead to aspiration pneumonia, pneumothorax, respiratory failure, cardiac arrhythmias, hypotension, pulmonary edema, myocarditis, convulsions, cerebral edema, polyneuropathy, and gastrointestinal ulceration.
section_summaries.diagnosis: Rabies encephalomyelitis can be rapidly confirmed during life using tests on skin biopsy or saliva samples. Antigen detection via IFA on frozen sections of skin biopsy and virus isolation or antigen detection from saliva or throat swabs are useful, with daily repetition until diagnosis confirmed. RT-PCR-based tests are sensitive but less specific than IFAT on skin biopsies. Diagnosis can be made during life, but lack of facilities often hinders confirmation. In developing countries, diagnosis relies on clinical features like hydrophobic spasms. Paralytic disease is harder to identify and frequently misdiagnosed globally. Neutralizing antibody tests on serum or CSF are diagnostic in unvaccinated patients; in vaccinated individuals, a sample should be saved for comparison. Post-mortem brain samples (needle necropsy or autopsy of brainstem/cerebellum) allow virus isolation, antigen detection (IFA impression smear), and RT-PCR. Rabies-related viruses are clinically indistinguishable from classic rabies, and diagnostic IFAT may be weakly positive or negative. Differential diagnosis includes psychiatric disease, hysteria, malingering, rabies phobia, tetanus, other encephalitides, and various poisons/drugs. Paralytic rabies must be differentiated from rapidly ascending flaccid paralysis syndromes like Guillain-Barré syndrome, transverse myelitis, and poliomyelitis.
section_summaries.treatment: Experimentally, no treatment has proven effective for rabies. For unvaccinated patients infected by dog rabies, palliation with heavy sedation and analgesia to relieve symptoms is recommended, along with post-exposure prophylaxis for contacts. Intensive care therapy for dog rabies virus infection in unvaccinated people has universally been fatal. Clinically, American insectivorous bat strains of rabies genotype/species 1 viruses appear less pathogenic, with one vaccinated and one unvaccinated patient recovering after intensive care. Previously vaccinated patients given intensive care may have a remote chance of survival, but with severe neurologic sequelae, and ICT should be considered for those with rabies-neutralizing antibody within the first week of illness, American bat rabies infections at an early stage, or those previously vaccinated. Effective anti-viral methods may be discovered in the future.
section_summaries.prevention: Ninety-nine percent of human deaths from rabies could be prevented by controlling dog rabies transmission through mass vaccination campaigns and education. Pre-exposure prophylaxis is recommended for individuals at risk (veterinarians, lab workers, animal handlers, travelers to enzootic areas). This involves an IM tissue culture vaccine dose on days 0, 7, and 28 (or an alternative 0.1mL ID dose for affordability). Shortened pre-exposure regimens (2 visits on days 0 and 7, IM or two-site ID) are also recommended. Booster doses are given based on risk level, unnecessary if neutralizing antibody is detectable. Post-exposure prophylaxis involves immediate treatment, even if delayed, including wound care (scrubbing with soap/detergent, rinsing, povidone-iodine irrigation, avoiding or delaying sutures). Passive immunization with rabies immunoglobulin (RIG) provides immediate temporary therapy, injected into/around the wound (20 units/kg human RIG or 40 units/kg equine RIG). Post-exposure vaccine regimen (Essen) is 4 doses on days 0, 3, 7, and 14-28 (IM). An economical 4-site ID regimen on day 0, followed by 2 ID injections on day 7 and a single ID dose on day 28, is also available. Previously vaccinated individuals do not need RIG and receive IM cell culture vaccine on days 0 and 3, or a single-day 4-site ID regimen. Combined active and passive immunization with optimal wound care reduces rabies risk from 15-60% to nearly 0%. Prophylaxis may fail if delayed, incomplete, or if the vaccinee is immunosuppressed. Rabies vaccines are less effective against phylogroup I rabies-related viruses and ineffective against Mokola virus. Pre-exposure immunization followed by post-exposure boosting is 100% effective in humans. Control of rabies in animal reservoirs through mass vaccination campaigns has led to fewer human cases in some settings.
